# Small Sample Properties of OLS

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=1000px></html>

## Small sample property of OLS estimators

### Small sample property (in general)

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Let's set up what this lecture is asking. An estimator is a function of data: hand it a sample, it hands you back a number. A small sample property is something you can say about that estimator before you have any data at all. That is a strange idea at first, so sit with it. We are not asking whether one particular estimate is right, because we can never know that. We are asking what kind of behaviour the rule has across all the samples you might have drawn. And the word small is misleading: these properties hold at any sample size.

</details>

**What is an estimator?** 

+ A function of data that produces an estimate (actual number) of a parameter of interest once you plug in actual values of data

+ OLS estimators: $\widehat{\beta}_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}$

<br>

**What is small sample property?**

Properties that hold whatever the sample size (small or large) is <span style = "color: red;"> prior to </span> obtaining actual estimates (before getting data)

+ Put more simply: what can you expect from the estimators before you actually get data and obtain estimates?

+ Difference between small sample property and the algebraic properties we looked at earlier?

### OLS?

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is the question that motivates the whole lecture. OLS is just one way of turning data into estimates. I could invent a dozen others by lunchtime. So why this one? What makes it worth teaching, and worth being the default in every statistical package on earth? The answer comes in two parts, which are the two bullets on screen. Unbiasedness, which is about whether the estimator is centred on the truth. And efficiency, which is about how tightly it clusters. We take each in turn, and the verdict is favourable.

</details>

OLS is just <span style = "color: red;"> a </span> way of using available information to obtain estimates. Does it have desirable properties? Why are we using it?

+ Unbiasedness
+ Efficiency

As it turns out, OLS is a very good way of using available information!!

:::
<!--end of panel-->

## Unbiasedness of OLS estimator

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Unbiasedness

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Before doing this for OLS, let's do it somewhere simpler, where you already have intuition. Suppose you only want the expected value of a variable, and your estimator is the sample mean. The code draws a hundred numbers from a standard normal, whose true mean is zero, and averages them. Now do what the direction box says and run it several times. You will not get zero. You will get zero point one, then minus zero point zero four, then zero point zero eight. That scatter is the point. No single run gives you the truth, and yet the sample mean is still a good estimator.

</details>

What does <span style = "color: blue;"> unbiased </span> even mean?

Let's first look at a simple problem of estimating the expected value of a single variable ($x$) as a start.

+ A good estimator of an expected value of a random variable is sample mean: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i^n x_i$

**R code: Sample Mean**

```{webr-r}
#--- set the number of observations ---#
n <- 100

#--- generate random values ---#
x_seq <- rnorm(n) # Normal(mean=0,sd=1)

#--- calculate the mean ---#
mean(x_seq)
```

<br>

:::{.callout-note title="Direction"}
Try running the codes multiple times and feel the tendency of the estimates.
:::

### Unbiased v.s. Biased

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is what running it a thousand times looks like. The top panel is our sample mean, and the whole distribution of estimates piles up around the red line, which is the true value of zero. That is unbiasedness: not that any one estimate is right, but that the distribution is centred on the truth. The bottom panel is what bias looks like, the same spread shifted across by zero point two. And notice that a biased estimator is not a noisier one. It can be beautifully precise and still systematically wrong, which is the more dangerous failure, because tight results look convincing.

</details>

```{webr-r}
#| autorun: true
#| context: output
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| out-width: 70%
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.8

#--- set seed ---#
set.seed(28394)

#--- set the number of observations ---#
n <- 100
B <- 1000
mean_st <- rep(0, B)
for (i in 1:B) {
  #--- generate random values ---#
  x_seq <- rnorm(n) # Normal(mean=0,sd=1)

  #--- calculate the mean ---#
  mean_st[i] <- mean(x_seq)
}
#--- the "biased" panel is the same draws shifted by 0.2, purely to show what
#--- bias looks like: a sampling distribution centred away from the truth
bias_size <- 0.2
plot_data_1 <- data.table(x = mean_st, type = "unbiased")
plot_data_2 <- data.table(x = mean_st + bias_size, type = paste0("biased (by ", bias_size, ")"))
plot_data <- rbind(plot_data_1, plot_data_2)

g_biased <-
  ggplot(data = plot_data) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(x = x),
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_grid(type ~ .) +
  xlab("Sample Mean") +
  #--- name the line, so it is clear what the distributions are centred on ---#
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0, y = Inf, label = "true value",
    color = "red", vjust = 1.6, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5
  ) +
  theme_lecture +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

g_biased
```

### Unbiasedness of OLS estimators

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Now the claim for OLS itself, and it is the same statement in symbols. The expected value of beta-one-hat equals beta-one. Take the expectation across all the samples you might have drawn, and you land on the truth. But note the phrase in blue: under certain conditions. This is not automatic, and those conditions are two tabs away. The parenthetical is worth reading too. We say nothing about the intercept, because almost nobody has ever cared about the intercept, and our time is short.

</details>

Under <span style = "color: blue;"> certain conditions </span>, OLS estimators are unbiased. That is,

$$
\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
E[\widehat{\beta}_1]=E\Big[\frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})^2}\Big]=\beta_1
$$

(We do not talk about unbiasedness of $\widehat{\beta}_0$ because we are almost never interested in the intercept. Given the limited time we have, it is not worthwhile talking about it)

### Seeing it

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Let's not take the algebra on faith. This does for OLS exactly what we did for the sample mean. I build a world where the true beta-one is two, draw a hundred observations, run the regression, keep the estimate, then repeat a thousand times. What you see is the resulting pile of estimates. Look at the spread: plenty of runs come back at one point seven, or two point three. Any one of them, on its own, is wrong. Now read the callout, because it is the whole idea. Unbiasedness is a claim about where the red line sits relative to the pile, not about any single estimate.

</details>

We did this for the sample mean two tabs ago. Here it is for the estimator this lecture is actually about: draw a fresh sample, run OLS, keep $\widehat{\beta}_1$, and repeat 1,000 times. The true $\beta_1$ is $2$.

```{webr-r}
#| context: output
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| out-width: 75%
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 6.1

set.seed(9382)

beta_1_true <- 2
B <- 1000
n <- 100
b1_st <- rep(0, B)

for (i in 1:B) {
  x <- rnorm(n) * 3
  u <- rnorm(n) * 5 #* satisfies E[u|x] = 0 by construction
  y <- 10 + beta_1_true * x + u
  b1_st[i] <- coef(lm(y ~ x))["x"]
}

ggplot(data = data.table(b1 = b1_st)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = b1), alpha = 0.5, color = "blue", bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_1_true, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  xlab("Estimate of beta_1") +
  theme_lecture
```

:::{.callout-note title="What to take from it"}
Individual estimates land all over the place &mdash; some well above $2$, some well below. Unbiasedness is <span style = "color: red;"> not </span> a claim about any one of them. It is the claim that the red line sits at the centre of the pile.
:::

### Conditions

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### SLR.1

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Four conditions buy us unbiasedness, and here is the first. Linear in parameters: in the population, y really is beta-zero plus beta-one x plus u. Notice what this is and is not saying. It is an assumption about the world, not about your data or your method. And the word linear refers to the parameters, not to x. You are allowed to put x squared or log x on the right-hand side and still be linear in this sense, which is lecture seven. If the world genuinely is not of this form, everything downstream is estimating something that does not exist.

</details>


:::{.callout-note title="Linear in Parameters"}
In the population model, the dependent variable, $y$, is related to the independent variable, $x$, and the error (or disturbance), $u$, as

$$
y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+u 
$$
:::

**Note**: This definition is from the textbook by Wooldridge

#### SLR.2

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Second, random sampling. Your n observations have to be drawn at random from the population you claim to be studying. The example on screen is the classic failure: you observe income and education only for people earning above twenty-five thousand. You have not sampled the population, you have sampled a slice of it, chosen using the very outcome you are studying. The distinction in red is worth keeping. Sampling on something unrelated to your question is largely harmless, which is what exogenous means here. Sampling on the outcome, or on the error, is endogenous, and it will bias you.

</details>

:::{.callout-note title="Random sampling"}
We have a random sample of size $n$, ${(x_i,y_i):i=1,2,\dots,n}$, following the population model.
:::

**Non-random sampling**

+ Example: You observe income-education data only for those who have income higher than $\$25K$
+ Benevolent and malevolent kinds:
  + <span style = "color: red;"> exogenous </span> sampling
  + <span style = "color: red;"> endogenous </span> sampling
+ We discuss this in more detail later

#### SLR.3

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Third, and this is the gentlest of the four: x cannot take the same value for everybody. Look back at the formula for beta-one-hat and you will see why immediately. The denominator is the sum of squared deviations of x from its mean. If every x is identical, that denominator is zero and you are dividing by nothing. Intuitively it is even more obvious. If nobody in your sample differs in x, the data contains no information at all about what happens when x changes. R will simply refuse, which makes this the friendliest condition to check.

</details>

:::{.callout-note title="Variation in covariates"}
The sample outcomes on $x$, namely, ${x_i,i=1,\dots,n}$, are not all the same value.
:::

#### SLR.4

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Fourth, and this is the one that will occupy the rest of your career: zero conditional mean. The expected value of u given x is zero, so whatever value of x you look at, the unobservables average out to the same thing. You met this last lecture. Combined with random sampling it applies observation by observation, which is the second equation. Zero conditional mean implies that x and u are uncorrelated, but the reverse is not generally true. Of the four conditions, three are comparatively easy to check or satisfy. This one cannot be verified from the observed data alone, and it is where the rest of this course lives.

</details>

:::{.callout-note title="Zero conditional mean"}
The error term $u$ has an expected value of zero given any value of the explanatory variable. In other words,

$$
E[u|x]=0  
$$
:::

Along with random sampling condition, this implies that

$$
E[u_i|x_i]=0 
$$

:::{.callout-important title="Necessary but not sufficient"}
$E[u|x]=0$ implies that $x$ is uncorrelated with $u$. Zero correlation by itself does not imply $E[u|x]=0$.
:::

:::
<!--end of panel-->

### (Math) Why OLS is unbiased

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Step 1: rewrite the estimator

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

This is the proof, in three steps, and it is worth following once. We start from the OLS formula and clean it up. The first move drops y-bar out of the numerator, which is legitimate because the sum of x-i minus x-bar is zero, so anything multiplied by it disappears. Then we name the denominator SST-x, purely to keep the writing short. Then comes the substitution that matters: replace y-i with what the model says it is, beta-zero plus beta-one x-i plus u-i. That is the step where the truth enters the algebra.

</details>

$$
\def\sumn{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\beta}_1 = & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2}  \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2} \;\; \Big[\text{because }\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y}=0\Big]\\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{SST_x} \;\;\Big[\text{where,}\;\; SST_x=\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2\Big]  \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})(\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i+u_i)}{SST_x} \\\\
= & \frac{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})\beta_0 +\sumn \beta_1(x_i-\bar{x})x_i+\sumn(x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x} 
\end{aligned}
$$


#### Step 2: simplify

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Now we tidy up the three pieces. The first has beta-zero multiplied by the sum of x-i minus x-bar, and we just said that sum is zero, so the whole term vanishes. The second contains the sum of x-i minus x-bar times x-i, and there is a small identity worth knowing: that equals the sum of squared deviations, which is SST-x itself. So the second term collapses to beta-one times SST-x over SST-x, which is simply beta-one. Everything has cancelled except beta-one and one remaining term built out of the errors.

</details>

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\beta}_1 = & \frac{\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})\beta_0 + \beta_1 \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})x_i+\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \text{Since } & \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})=0\;\; \text{and}\\
    & \sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})x_i=\sumn  (x_i-\bar{x})^2=SST_x,
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\beta_1 SST_x+\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i}{SST_x} 
  = \beta_1+(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Step 3: take expectations

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

And here is the punchline, on a single line. Beta-one-hat equals beta-one, plus a term made entirely out of the error terms. The estimator is the truth plus contamination. So take expectations conditional on the x values. Beta-one is a constant and passes through untouched. The second term survives only through the expected value of u-i given x. Set that to zero, which is exactly condition four, and it vanishes, leaving beta-one. Read the note: when there is bias, it is precisely that surviving term. This algebra is behind every warning I will give you this semester.

</details>

$$\widehat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1+(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i$$

The estimator is the truth plus a term built entirely out of the errors. Taking the expectation of $\widehat{\beta}_1$ conditional on $\mathbf{x}=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$,

$$
\begin{align}
\Rightarrow E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}] = & E[\beta_1|\mathbf{x}]+E[(1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})u_i|\mathbf{x}]  \\\\
= & \beta_1 + (1/SST_x)\sumn (x_i-\bar{x}) E[u_i|\mathbf{x}]
\end{align}
$$

So, if condition 4 $(E[u_i|\mathbf{x}]=0)$ is satisfied, that second term vanishes:

$$
\def\Ex{E_{\mathbf{x}}}
\begin{align}
E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}] = & \beta_1 \\\\
\Ex\big[E[\widehat{\beta}_1|\mathbf{x}]\big] = & E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1
\end{align}
$$

:::{.callout-note}
Notice which condition did the work: <span style = "color: red;"> SLR.4 </span>, zero conditional mean. Break that one and the second term does not vanish, and its value is the bias.
:::

:::
<!--end of panel-->

:::
<!--end of panel-->


## Unbiasedness of OLS in practice

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Good empiricists

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

So what does all this mean for you, as somebody who will actually run these regressions? Three things, and not one of them is mathematical. You have to be able to judge whether those four conditions hold in your particular setting, because nobody else can do it for you; it depends on the institutions and the behaviour that generated your data. You have to know what to do when one of them fails. And underneath both, you have to know your context well enough to make the call. That is why economists specialise in fields rather than in estimators.

</details>

Good empiricists

+ have ability to judge if the above conditions are satisfied for the particular context you are working on

+ have ability to correct (if possible) for the problems associated with the violations of any of the above conditions

+ knows the context well so you can make appropriate judgments

### Unbiasedness of OLS estimators

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Let's practise that judgement on the regression from last lecture. Price on lot size, with u holding everything else. Take the two questions seriously. What is in u? Location, above all, but also the number of bedrooms, the condition of the house, whether there is a garage. Now the second question, which decides whether your estimate means anything at all. Is any of that correlated with lot size? Think about where the large lots are. They are in the suburbs, and suburban houses differ from downtown houses in a dozen ways at once. So no, I do not believe this one.

</details>

**Reconsider the following example**

$$
price=\beta_0+\beta_1\times lotsize + u 
$$

+ $price$: house price (USD)
+ $lotsize$: lot size
+ $u$: error term (everything else)

**Questions**

+ What's in $u$?
+ Do you think $E[u|x]=0$ is satisfied? In other words (roughly speaking), is $u$ uncorrelated with $x$? 

### Let me reiterate

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

I want to close this section by being blunt about what unbiasedness does not give you. It says nothing whatever about the estimate sitting in front of you. Go back to that pile of simulated estimates: the estimator there was perfectly unbiased, and there were still runs that came back badly wrong. Yours could be one of them, and no diagnostic will tell you. What unbiasedness buys is a guarantee about the procedure, not about the result. That is genuinely worth having, but it is weaker than most people assume when they report a coefficient.

</details>

+ Unbiasedness property of OLS estimators says <span style = "color: blue;"> nothing </span> about the estimate that we obtain for a given sample

+ It is always possible that we could obtain an unlucky sample that would give us a point estimate far from $\beta_1$, and we can never know for sure whether this is the case.

:::
<!--end of panel-->

## Variance of OLS estimator

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Introduction

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

That brings us to the second property, and to the natural next question. If estimates scatter, how much do they scatter? OLS estimators are random variables, not because there is anything mystical about them, but simply because they are computed from data, and a different sample gives a different number. The variance of an OLS estimator measures how wide that pile of estimates is. Unbiasedness told us where the pile is centred. Variance tells us how tightly it is packed. You want both: centred on the truth, and narrow.

</details>

+ OLS estimators are random variables because $y$, $x$, and $u$ are random variables (this just means that you do not know the estimates until you get samples). 

+ Variance of OLS estimators is a measure of how much spread in estimates (realized values) you will get.

+ We let $Var(\widehat{\beta}_{OLS})$ denote the variance of the OLS estimators of $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$.

### Variance (example)

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is why variance matters even when bias does not. Two estimators of the same expected value. The smart one averages all thousand observations. The naive one averages the first ten and throws the other nine hundred and ninety away. Both are unbiased, as the line above the figure says, so on the criterion we spent the last section on they are tied. Now look at the picture. The smart estimator's distribution is a narrow spike; the naive one is a wide hill. Same centre, wildly different reliability. Unbiasedness on its own would happily let you pick the bad one.

</details>

Consider two estimators of $E[x]$:

```{=tex}
\begin{align}
\theta_{smart} = & \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i  \;\;(n=1000) \\\\
\theta_{naive} = & \frac{1}{10} \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i
\end{align}
```

Both are unbiased &mdash; the naive one simply throws away 990 of the 1000 observations.

**Variance of the estimators**

```{webr-r}
#| context: output
#| message: false 
#| warning: false 
#| out-width: 60%
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 4.9
 
set.seed(38495)

B <- 1000
theta_smart <- rep(0, B)
theta_naive <- rep(0, B)
for (i in 1:B) {
  x <- rnorm(1000)
  theta_smart[i] <- mean(x)
  theta_naive[i] <- mean(x[1:10])
}

smart_data <- data.table(value = theta_smart, type = "Smart")
naive_data <- data.table(value = theta_naive, type = "Naive")
plot_data <- rbind(smart_data, naive_data)

ggplot(data = plot_data) +
  geom_density(aes(x = value, fill = type), alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_discrete(name = "Estimator") +
  xlab("Sample Mean") +
  theme_lecture +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

### Variance of OLS estimator

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is the formula, and it is simple enough to memorise. The variance of beta-one-hat is sigma squared over SST-x. Sigma squared is the variance of the error term; SST-x is the total variation in your explanatory variable. Note the condition attached at the top: this requires the variance of u given x to be constant, which has a name we meet shortly. Below is the standard error, which is just the square root of the variance. Standard error is the phrase you will actually see in output, and it is the number that decides whether anyone believes your coefficient.

</details>

**(True) Variance of the OLS Estimator**

If $Var(u|x)=\sigma^2$ and the four conditions (we used to prove unbiasedness of the OLS estimator) are satisfied,

$$
\begin{align}
  Var(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sumn (x_i-\bar{x})^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_x} 
\end{align}
$$

<br>

**(TRUE) Standard Error of the OLS Estimator**

The standard error of the OLS estimator is just a square root of the variance of the OLS estimator. We use $se(\widehat{\beta}_1)$ to denote it.

$$
\begin{aligned}
  se(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sqrt{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{SST_x}} 
\end{aligned}
$$

### What affects $Var(\widehat{\beta}_{OLS})$?

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Two lessons come straight out of that formula, and both are practical. First, the noisier the world, meaning a bigger sigma squared, the less precise your estimate. That one you can rarely do anything about. Second, and this is the useful one, the more your x varies, the smaller the variance. Look at where SST-x sits: in the denominator. So if you are designing an experiment, spread your treatment values as widely as you can. Do not test nitrogen rates of a hundred and a hundred and ten. And as the last bullet admits, most of the time you inherit your data and have no such luxury.

</details>

**Variance of the OLS estimators** 

$$Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x) = \sigma^2/SST_x$$

<br>

**What can you learn from this equation?**

+ the variance of OLS estimators is smaller (larger) if the variance of error term is smaller (larger)

+ the greater (smaller) the variation in the covariate $x$, the smaller (larger) the variance of OLS estimators

    - if you are running experiments, spread the value of $x$ as much as possible
    - you will rarely have this luxury

:::
<!--end of panel-->

## Efficiency of OLS Estimators

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Nature of error term

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Two words you will hear constantly, so let's define them precisely. Homoskedasticity: the variance of the error term is the same at every value of x, so the spread of the unobservables does not depend on where you are along the x axis. Heteroskedasticity: it does depend on x, so the variance is some function of x. That is the entire distinction. And notice that neither says anything about the average of the error; that was condition four, and it is a separate matter. This is about spread, not centre, and the next tab draws both.

</details>

**Homoskedasticity**

The error $u$ has the same variance given any value of the covariate $x$ $(Var(u|x)=\sigma^2)$

<br>

**Heteroskedasticity**

The variance of the error $u$ differs depending on the value of $x$ $(Var(u|x)=f(x))$

### Visualization

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here they are side by side, both generated from the same true line. In the top panel the cloud has a constant thickness: the band of points is as wide at x equals fifty as it is at x equals two hundred. That is homoskedastic. In the bottom panel the cloud fans out; at low x the points hug the line, at high x they scatter far above and below. That is heteroskedastic. Now look at the line itself in both panels. It is the same line, correctly placed. Heteroskedasticity does not move your estimate. It changes how confident you are entitled to be about it.

</details>

```{webr-r}
#| context: output
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 6.6
 
x_levels <- seq(40, 200, by = 10)
x <- rep(x_levels, each = 200)

u_homoske <- rnorm(200 * length(x_levels)) * 20
y_homoske <- 100 + 0.5 * x + u_homoske

u_hetero <- lapply(x_levels, function(x) rnorm(200, sd = x / 50) * 20) %>% unlist()
y_hetero <- 100 + 0.5 * x + u_hetero

plot_data_homo <-
  data.table(
    x = x,
    y = y_homoske
  ) %>%
  .[, type := "Homoskedastic"]

plot_data_hetero <-
  data.table(
    x = x,
    y = y_hetero
  ) %>%
  .[, type := "Heteroskedastic"]

plot_data <- rbind(plot_data_homo, plot_data_hetero)

g_error_nature <- 
  ggplot(data = plot_data) +
  geom_point(aes(y = y, x = x), size = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 100, slope = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  facet_grid(type ~ .) +
  theme_lecture

g_error_nature
```

### House Price Example

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

And here is the same thing in data nobody manufactured. Look at the left-hand side of the cloud, at the small lot sizes: those prices sit inside a fairly narrow band. Now look at the right, at the large lots, where prices are scattered enormously, from quite cheap to very expensive. That fanning shape is heteroskedasticity in the wild, and it is what you should expect to find. It makes sense, too: big lots come in far more varieties than small ones. The lesson to carry forward is that homoskedasticity is the unusual case, not the default.

</details>

The previous tab was manufactured. Here is the same thing in real data: look at how the vertical spread of the points <span style = "color: red;"> widens </span> as lot size grows. Small lots sell within a narrow band; large lots are all over the place. That is heteroskedasticity, and it is the normal case, not the exception.

```{webr-r}
#| context: output
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-width: 10.2
#| fig-height: 6.6
 
data(HousePrices, package = "AER")

g_hp <-
  ggplot(data = HousePrices) +
  geom_point(aes(y = price, x = lotsize), size = 0.6) +
  ylab("House Price ($)") +
  xlab("Lot Size") +
  theme_lecture

g_hp +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = price, x = lotsize), method = "lm", se = F)
```

### Gauss-Markov Theorem

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

This theorem is the formal answer to why we use OLS. Under the four conditions plus homoskedasticity, which gets called SLR point five, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator, BLUE. But read the qualifiers box, because that sentence gets quoted far too loosely. Best means smallest variance. And it holds only within the class of estimators that are linear in y and unbiased. It is not a claim that nothing beats OLS. Give up the unbiasedness requirement and estimators with smaller variance do exist, which is a trade more advanced methods are happy to make.

</details>

:::{.callout-note title="Gauss-Markov Theorem"}
Under conditions $SLR.1$ through $SLR.4$ and the <span style = "color: blue;"> homoskedasticity </span> assumption ($SLR.5$), OLS estimators are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUEs)
:::

<br>

**In other words,**

No other <span style = "color: blue;"> unbiased linear </span> estimators have smaller variance than the OLS estimators (desirable efficiency property of OLS)

:::{.callout-note title="Read the qualifiers"}
"Best" here means smallest variance, and only <span style = "color: red;"> within </span> the class of estimators that are both linear in $y$ and unbiased. It does not say OLS beats everything. Drop the unbiasedness requirement and estimators with smaller variance do exist &mdash; that is the trade we make in more advanced methods.
:::

### Notes

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Two things to keep straight, because they get conflated constantly. First, homoskedasticity is not needed for unbiasedness. Go back through the proof and you will see only condition four did any work there, so heteroskedasticity does not bias your coefficients. Second, and this is why we care, in most real applications homoskedasticity fails; you just saw it in the house price scatter. What that breaks is the variance formula, and therefore the standard errors, and therefore every test you run. Your estimate is fine. Your confidence in it is not. Lecture six is entirely about this.

</details>

+ We do <span style = "color: red;"> NOT </span> need the homoskedasticity condition to prove that OLS estimators are unbiased

+ In most applications, homoskedasticity condition is not satisfied, which has important implications on:
    - estimation of variance (standard error) of OLS estimators
    - significance test

(<span style = "color: red;"> A lot more on this issue later </span>)

:::
<!--end of panel-->


## Estimating the variance of error 

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Why?

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

A short tab with a large motivation behind it. We have a formula for the variance of beta-one-hat, but it contains sigma squared, which is a feature of the population and therefore unknown. So we need to estimate it. And the reason we bother is right there on the screen: once you can estimate that variance, you can test whether beta-one is statistically distinguishable from zero. Every p-value you have ever seen in a regression table runs through this quantity. So the next few tabs are the plumbing behind the most-read column of every results table in economics.

</details>

Once you estimate $Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x)$, you can test the statistical significance of $\widehat{\beta}_1$ (More on this later)

### Problem

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is the obstacle, laid out in steps. We know the variance of beta-one-hat is sigma squared over SST-x. SST-x is fine, because it is built from x, which you observe. So everything hinges on sigma squared, the variance of the error. And there is a natural estimator for that: since the error has mean zero, its variance is the expected value of u squared, so you would just average the squared errors. The logic is sound line by line. Then the last bullet pulls the rug out. We never observe u. Read the fragment, which is the way out: we do observe the residuals.

</details>

+ We know that $Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x) = \sigma^2/SST_x$.

+ You can calculate $SST_x$ because $x$ is observable. So, as long as we know $\sigma^2$, which is $Var(u)$ (the variance of the error term), then we know $Var(\widehat{\beta}_1|x)$. 

+ Since $Var(u_i)=\sigma^2=E[u_i^2] \;\; \Big( Var(u_i)\equiv E[u_i^2]-E[u_i]^2 \Big)$, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^2$ is an unbiased estimator of $Var(u_i)$

+ Unfortunately, we don't observe $u_i$ (error)

::: {.fragment}
:::{.callout-note title="But,"}
We observe $\widehat{u_i}$ (residuals)!! Can we use residuals instead?
:::
:::
<!--end of the fragment-->

### Proposal

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

So the obvious move is to substitute what we have for what we want, and use u-hat, the residual, wherever the formula asks for u, the error. It is not an unreasonable move, because the expected difference between a residual and its error is zero; the proof is in the last tab of this slide if you want it. So the proposal is to average the squared residuals. Then read the final line, which is the twist: that estimator is biased. Not fatally, and not mysteriously. The next tab explains exactly where the problem comes from.

</details>

We know $E[\widehat{u}_i-u_i]=0$ (the proof is in the <span style = "color: blue;"> (Math) Residual vs error </span> tab at the end of this slide), so, why don't we use $\widehat{u}_i$ (observable) in place of $u_i$ (unobservable)?

<br>

::: {.fragment}
:::{.callout-note title="Proposed Estimator of $\sigma^2$"}
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2$
:::

:::
<!--end of the fragment-->

<br>

::: {.fragment}
Unfortunately, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{u}_i^2$ is a biased estimator of $\sigma^2$
:::
<!--end of the fragment-->

### Algebraic property of OLS

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

Here is the reason, and it goes back to the first-order conditions we derived last lecture. OLS guarantees two equations always hold: the residuals sum to zero, and x times the residuals sums to zero. Now think about what that means as bookkeeping. If I tell you n minus two of the residuals, you can solve those two equations for the remaining two. They are not free to be anything at all. So although you appear to have n residuals in front of you, only n minus two of them carry independent information. Two were spent estimating the intercept and the slope.

</details>

**FOCs of the minimization problem OLS solves**

```{=tex}
\begin{align}
    \sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i=0\;\; \text{and}\;\; \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\widehat{u}_i=0\notag
\end{align}
```

+ this means that once you know the value of $n-2$ residuals, you can find the value of the other two by solving the above equations
+ so, it's almost as if you have $n-2$ value of residuals instead of $n$

### Unbiased estimator 

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

And that is the fix: divide by n minus two rather than by n. That single change makes the estimator unbiased, compensating exactly for the two degrees of freedom you spent. From there it is bookkeeping. Put sigma-hat squared into the variance formula and you have the estimated variance of beta-one-hat; take its square root and you have the estimated standard error, which is the quantity printed in every regression table you will ever read. Notice the hats piling up. It is an estimate of the standard deviation of an estimator. Keep that sentence, because that is what a standard error is.

</details>

:::{.callout-note title="Unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$"}
$\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2$ $\;\;\;\;\;\;$($E[\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{u}_i^2]=\sigma^2$)
:::

<br>

Hereafter we use $\widehat{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)}$ to denote the <span style = "color: red;"> estimated </span> variance of the OLS estimator $\widehat{\beta}_1$, and it is defined as

$$
\widehat{Var(\widehat{\beta}_1)} = \widehat{\sigma}^2/SST_x
$$

<br>

Since $se(\widehat{\beta}_1)=\sigma/\sqrt{SST_x}$, the natural estimator of $se(\widehat{\beta_1})$ (<span style = "color: red;"> standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_1$ </span>) is

$$
\widehat{se(\widehat{\beta}_1)} =\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2}/\sqrt{SST_x},
$$

:::{.callout-note}
Later, we use $\widehat{se(\hat{\beta_1})}$ for testing.
:::

### R code

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

And here it is in practice. Run the regression with feols, call summary, and look at the column labelled standard error. That number is the sigma-hat over root SST-x we have just built, computed for you. Everything from the last twenty minutes sits behind that one column. Two things to notice. It sits right beside the estimate, and the ratio of the two is the t-value in the next column, which is the whole of lecture five. And by default this standard error assumes homoskedasticity, which we agreed two slides ago is usually false.

</details>

```{webr-r}
#--- run OLS on the above model ---#
# lm(dep_var ~ indep_var,data=data_name)
uni_reg <- fixest::feols(price ~ lotsize, data = HousePrices)

summary(uni_reg)
```

### (Math) Residual vs error

<details class="transcript">
<summary>Lecturer transcript</summary>

This is the proof I promised back on the Proposal tab, and the conditioning matters. Write the same y two ways: once with the true parameters and the error, once with the estimated parameters and the residual. Set them equal and rearrange. Conditional on the full set of observed x values, OLS is unbiased and each x-i is fixed, so both coefficient-estimation errors have conditional expectation zero. Therefore the residual minus the error also has conditional expectation zero. This does not mean their squares have the same expectation; that is why the degrees-of-freedom correction was necessary.

</details>

**Error and Residual** 

```{=tex}
\begin{align}
    y_i = \beta_0+\beta_1 x_i + u_i \\
    y_i = \hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1 x_i + \hat{u}_i 
\end{align}
```

**Residuals as unbiased estimators of error**

```{=tex}
\begin{align}
  \hat{u}_i & = y_i -\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1 x_i \\
  \hat{u}_i & = \beta_0+\beta_1 x_i + u_i -\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1 x_i \\
  \Rightarrow \hat{u}_i -u_i & = (\beta_0-\hat{\beta}_0)+(\beta_1-\hat{\beta}_1) x_i \\
  \Rightarrow E[\hat{u}_i-u_i|\mathbf{x}] & = E[(\beta_0-\hat{\beta}_0)+(\beta_1-\hat{\beta}_1)x_i|\mathbf{x}]=0
\end{align}
```
:::
<!--end of panel-->
